title: Nonstabilizerness of the entangling layer in quantum circuit Born machines
abstract: The entangling layer of a quantum circuit Born machine can supply both entanglement and nonstabilizerness. In this work we show that the entangling layer can be a Clifford circuit, which supplies no nonstabilizerness. We use an architecture in which a fixed, non-trainable entangler is reused in every layer and only single-qubit rotations are optimized. There, a Clifford entangler reaches the same Kullback--Leibler divergence as a near-Haar one at sufficient circuit depth, and entanglers spanning zero to Haar-typical nonstabilizerness reach the same loss, up to a small offset for a free-fermion matchgate entangler. A doping control that raises the entangler's nonstabilizerness while leaving the entangling power of every gate unchanged leaves the loss flat. With a Clifford entangler the nonstabilizerness of the trained state comes entirely from the rotations, which take the trained circuit outside the stabilizer formalism. We also show that, among all pure states whose Born distribution is a given target, the one whose amplitudes are the positive square roots of the probabilities has the smallest stabilizer Rényi entropy, so this minimum can be computed without training.
summary: This work analyzes quantum circuit Born machines to determine if the entangling layer must introduce nonstabilizerness to generate complex probability distributions. The authors demonstrate that simple Clifford entanglers can achieve the same simulation accuracy as complex Haar-random ones. This suggests that the ability to generate entanglement is more critical than the explicit introduction of nonstabilizerness.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the entangling layer in a quantum circuit Born machine must inherently supply nonstabilizerness, independent of its ability to generate entanglement.
main_result: A Clifford entangler can achieve the same generative loss (KLD) as a near-Haar entangler, suggesting that nonstabilizerness is not strictly necessary for good state preparation.
method: The authors analyze the circuit using the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) as a loss function and the Stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) as a diagnostic for nonstabilizerness.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum circuit Born machine, which approximates a target probability distribution $q_	heta(x)$ by interleaving trainable single-qubit rotations with a fixed, reusable entangling layer $\hat{U}_S$.
key_observables: Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD), Stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE), and the minimum nonstabilizerness $M_{2, \min}(p)$.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($L$), doping parameter ($n_t$), and the structure of the target distribution (e.g., Gaussian mixtures, SK model).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the fixed entangler is reused across all layers, and the minimum nonstabilizerness is achieved by the state whose amplitudes are the positive square roots of the probabilities.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the circuit structure with trainable rotations and the fixed entangler. Other figures compare KLD convergence across different entangler families (Clifford vs. Haar) and show the correlation between doping and loss.
paper_structure: The paper first defines the Born machine setup and compares different entangler families (Clifford, Local-Haar, etc.). It then analyzes the loss convergence, showing that Clifford entanglers suffice. Finally, it derives that the minimum nonstabilizerness is achieved by the positive square-root state, a result computable without training.
why_interesting: It provides a theoretical understanding of the necessary complexity (nonstabilizerness) required in quantum circuits to simulate complex probability distributions, offering insights into the resource requirements for quantum machine learning.
